description: terra.pura is a project linking NASA data, financial statistics and agriculture together, helping independent farmers plan for the future.
summary: Technology in agriculture is heavily dominated by already enormous & thriving companies, and we don't see enough technology that is free & easy-to-use given to independent farmers; so we created terra.pura! Our app allows anyone (maybe even including you) to learn a bit about your soil and region, while also being provided information backed by many sources (including NASA, independent surveyors and weather forecasts) on what to plant & when to achieve the best results. We also offer comprehensive tracking tools for independent farmers looking to sell their goods for a profit, allowing them to see how much they may need to invest in return for crops and a stable profit.
details:
What does terra.pura do and how does it work?

terra.pura turns satellite, climate and market data into a plain answer for one field: what is worth growing there right now, what it will really cost, how likely it is to succeed and how likely it is to sell. A farmer searches for their farm, drops a few pins around the field, chooses their energy and water providers, and adds the machinery and storage they have. terra.pura then builds a dashboard for that exact piece of land:

- Climate: 20+ years of NASA POWER data for the field (temperature, rainfall, sunlight, soil wetness), plus a 16-day Open-Meteo forecast.

- Soil: pH and fertility from ISRIC SoilGrids.

- Land health from orbit: NASA GIBS imagery (30 m Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 and the MODIS vegetation index, NDVI) shows how green the field is compared with a normal year. Healthy leaves absorb red light and reflect near-infrared, so the gap between the two reveals how well the crop is growing.

- Hazards: NASA EONET flags nearby wildfires, storms and floods, alongside frost and heat warnings from the forecast.

- Crop model: a day-by-day growth simulation (growing degree-days, an FAO-56 soil water balance, and frost, heat, drought, waterlogging and pH stress) runs over many simulated seasons to estimate how many plants survive and how big the harvest is.

- Costs and markets: energy, water, seeds, fuel, storage, fertiliser and labour are priced with the farmer's real local providers and wages. FAOSTAT and World Bank data show what the harvest is worth and how likely it is to sell.

What benefits does terra.pura have?

- A ranked list of crops to plant now, each with cost, sales, profit margin and risk of failure.

- A sped-up growth simulation showing which plants struggle, when and why.

- An itemised cost report, where every number shows how it was calculated and can be edited.

- Extra tools: a solar planner, a market page (demand and supply, and the odds of a supermarket contract), an on-farm processing calculator (flour mill or oil press), machinery emissions and satellite crop-health tracking.

- It's free, works worldwide in the farmer's own currency and needs no training. Optional accounts save up to five farms.

What is terra.pura's intended impact?

Planning tools like this are usually paid, scattered across separate services, or built for large agribusiness. We want independent and smallholder farmers to have the same Earth observation data, for free, so they can choose better crops, avoid losses and stay profitable as the climate grows less predictable. Because everything is open and explained, it also helps students and the public understand how satellite data connects to the food on their plate.

What tools, languages and frameworks were used?

- Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (ES modules, no framework) and Python.

- Libraries: Leaflet (maps) and three.js (interactive 3D crop models), both served from our own site.

- Server: a small Python server, using only the standard library, for optional accounts. It has a SQLite database and scrypt-hashed passwords.

- Data: NASA POWER, NASA GIBS (HLS, MODIS), NASA EONET, ISRIC SoilGrids, Open-Meteo, FAOSTAT, the World Bank Pink Sheet, OpenStreetMap, Wikidata (provider logos), and national energy and water regulators and providers.

- Hardware: no special hardware. It runs in any modern browser on a phone, tablet or computer.

- Super Intelligence (SI): the code was generated with Claude by Anthropic, working from our team's own designs, feature decisions and direction. We reviewed and tested every part.

How is terra.pura's project creative?

- It connects data that's normally kept apart. Satellite crop health, decades of climate, soil chemistry, local utility prices and national market data feed one decision, for one field.

- Instead of a static score, it simulates a season plant by plant, so farmers can watch where and why crops fail.

- Satellite NDVI is presented as "greener or browner than usual for this time of year", which anyone can understand.

- It doesn't stop at "what to grow". It follows the crop all the way to selling it and to processing it (flour or oil) on the farm.

- It uses each farmer's real local energy, water and sewage providers in over 100 countries, rather than one global average.

What factors did we consider?

- Accessibility: free, no account required, works on phones, plain-language explanations, and the farmer's own currency and units.

- Accuracy and honesty: every estimate shows its sources and assumptions, farmers can replace any figure with their own, and limits (such as 250 m satellite pixels on small fields) are stated openly.

- Privacy: farm data stays in the farmer's browser unless they choose to save it. Nothing is shared or sold, there are no trackers, and passwords are hashed.

- Reliability: maps and libraries are served from our own site so it works behind school and office web filters, and it falls back gracefully when a data service is busy.

- Global reach: climate and satellite data work anywhere. Prices, providers and markets cover as many countries as public data allows.

- Sustainability: machinery emissions, solar potential and water use are shown next to profit, so farmers can weigh both.
